A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-loss research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched reliably despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original DIP denoising, simulated PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution, sensitivity analyses and computational timing results.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds noise-misspecification experiments, a clinical 3D PET reconstruction and learned-prior image deblurring.

M1.justification: The core CDF–logit–Wasserstein loss and Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. Appendix G adds a concrete PnP-DC inference procedure that alternates Adam data updates, fixed DnCNN denoising and ADMM dual updates, extending the method beyond its previous implementations.

E1.justification: v2 adds a real clinical 3D PET scan, grayscale image deblurring with a learned prior, and denoising under outlier-contaminated, spatially correlated and intensity-dependent noise. These extend the represented data and inverse-problem conditions beyond the retained synthetic PET, denoising and 1D deconvolution experiments.

E2.justification: Appendix G introduces PnP-MSE with the same fixed DnCNN prior as the comparator for PnP-DC. The clinical comparison includes a vendor MLEM reconstruction. Existing DIP-MSE, NLL-Adam and synthetic MLEM comparisons remain; newly discussed robust losses and SURE are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include clinical PET reconstruction with 21 subsets, positivity projection and learning rate 10^-4, and PnP reconstruction with 2,500 ADMM iterations and five inner Adam steps. Appendix E.5 introduces controlled noise-mismatch sweeps. These are additional evaluation designs; the earlier experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 directly tests violations of the assumed noise model through outliers, spatial correlation and heteroscedasticity. Appendix G adds sensitivity analysis over the ADMM penalty. These substantially extend the earlier noise-level, measurement-count, voxel-size and TV-regularization analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-initialization DIP reporting, error bars described as 1.96 times standard deviation, 100-evaluation distribution checks and timing statistics over 1,000 runs. The added studies introduce no stated new replication, confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Appendix G newly reports peak PnP PSNR of 27.5 dB for DC versus 26.9 dB for MSE. Figures E14–E16 add mismatch results, including a substantially reduced advantage under correlated noise. Figure 9 adds clinical reconstructions, and Appendix F.5 reports 0.057 versus 0.037 seconds per iteration for DC-Adam and NLL-Adam. Earlier results are retained.

T1.justification: The displayed PET likelihood drops the unexplained additive background b: v1 Equation 8 uses Ax+b, whereas v2 Equation 7 uses Aθ, matching the stated synthetic forward model. This is a limited formula correction. The PIT proofs, error propositions, counterexample and tail derivations in Appendices A–C remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claims about distributional fidelity, reduced noise fitting and compatibility with regularization remain. v2 adds real 3D PET applicability as an explicit contribution and narrows the abstract's framing to unsupervised, noise-dominated inverse problems without paired training data.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly excludes problems dominated by large null spaces, such as inpainting, from its intended scope. It interprets PnP stability through reduced conflict between fidelity and the learned prior, and qualifies the clinical example as an initial feasibility demonstration. The earlier nonuniqueness and need-for-priors limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of a future anonymous repository with an explicit source-code address. It adds clinical scanner geometry, corrections, voxel dimensions, initialization, optimization and runtime details; noise-mismatch generation instructions; and PnP kernel, denoiser and optimization specifications. These substantially expand the documented reproduction information.

R1.justification: The brief v1 discussion linking DC to method noise and likelihood scheduling is replaced by expanded background positioning against robust losses, SURE, Noise2Noise, goodness-of-fit tests and early stopping. Section 2.2 particularly frames DC as an optimization-oriented analogue of classical goodness-of-fit criteria, substantially changing its relationship to prior research.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and Sections 3.1–3.2 around a clearer percentile/PIT explanation. Related work moves into the background with a different narrative, the DIP comparison explains peak-PSNR early stopping more explicitly, and the appendix guide is reorganized. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual evidence: clinical PET images in Figure 9, robustness curves with reconstruction panels in Figures E14–E16, and PnP sensitivity and reconstruction comparisons in Figures F8–F9. Retained figures are reflowed and some captions revised; Tables 1–2 retain their structure and values.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on synthetic corruption and correctly specified noise models. Controlled mismatch tests expose an important weakness under correlation, while clinical PET and learned-prior experiments test previously unverified applicability. Clearer scope, stronger research positioning and concrete reproduction details further improve the paper. The new clinical and PnP demonstrations remain single cases without broad uncertainty assessment, so they establish feasibility rather than general superiority, but the combined gains materially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation.
